units.title: Step time, token throughput and MFU versus HFU
outcomes: Define step time, tokens per second, MFU and HFU, stating the FLOP count and peak each ratio uses.
Derive tokens per second from step time and batch tokens, and MFU from model FLOPs over peak throughput.
Measure step time and tokens per second with warmup and synchronization, and label CPU timings as non-evidence for GPU interconnects.
units.why: Throughput numbers mean nothing without fixed workload semantics and stated FLOP counts. This unit fixes the definitions before any diagnosis.

next.note: Label the compute, memory or communication bound behind the throughput.
Extend single-rank throughput to scaling efficiency and failure-adjusted goodput.

study.title: Roofline diagnosis and the MFU definition
study.locator: The Memory Wall and Roofline Diagnosis with the iron law and ridge table, and Measurement at Scale with the MFU bands (40 to 60 percent good, above 60 excellent)

focus: Step time is wall-clock per optimizer step at fixed global batch, sequence length and precision. Tokens per second is global-batch tokens divided by step time.
MFU uses model FLOPs, commonly \(6 N D\) for training, over peak. HFU uses actual FLOPs including recomputation and padding. State both before comparing.
MFU is rough under mixed precision because regions run in different formats while the peak assumes one. Compare before and after on the same setup, never across clusters.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive tokens per second and MFU for \(N = 10^9\) parameters, \(D = 10^6\) tokens and \(T_{step} = 30\) s at peak \(989\) TFLOP/s: tokens/s is about 33,333, model FLOPs are \(6 \times 10^{15}\), achieved about 200 TFLOP/s, MFU about 20 percent.
traps: Comparing MFUs built from different FLOP counts (with versus without attention terms, forward-only versus training) or different peaks (sparse versus dense, BF16 versus FP16).
Reading CPU `gloo` step times as evidence about GPU throughput or interconnects. They check semantics only.
Treating `FlopCounterMode` as exact. It has performance and memory problems and serves as a cross-check, not the answer.

selfTest.q: How are step time, global-batch tokens and tokens per second related?
selfTest.a: Tokens per second is \(D_{tokens} / T_{step}\) at fixed batch, sequence and precision. Change any of the three and the ratio is incomparable.

selfTest.q: Why can HFU exceed MFU on the same run?
selfTest.a: HFU counts actual FLOPs including recomputation, padding and synchronization overhead. MFU counts model FLOPs only, so extra work raises HFU but not MFU.

selfTest.q: A paper reports 55.2 percent MFU on 12,288 GPUs. Can you compare your single-GPU MFU to it?
selfTest.a: No. Different hardware, FLOP-count convention and workload. The 55.2 percent figure is MegaScale's own cluster result for a 175B model, not a transferable target.

selfTest.q: Manual arithmetic and `FlopCounterMode` disagree. Which do you trust?
selfTest.a: The manual count with stated assumptions. The counter is a cross-check with known performance and memory issues.

units.title: Strong and weak scaling efficiency and goodput under failures
outcomes: Define strong scaling, weak scaling and parallel efficiency, stating the fixed quantity in each.
Derive goodput with failures, retries and unusable work for one job size from failure rate and restart cost.
Explain why high device utilization can coexist with poor useful throughput.
units.why: More ranks can raise utilization while lowering useful output once failures, restarts and stragglers dominate. This unit separates busy hardware from finished work.

next.note: Convert goodput into cost per useful token.
Turn failure math into health checks, canaries and runbooks.

study.title: MegaScale scaling and straggler evidence
study.locator: arXiv:2402.15627v1, Sections 4 to 6: heartbeat fault loop, straggler mitigation and 55.2 percent MFU on 12,288 GPUs for a 175B model

study.title: Failure taxonomy and MTTF versus job size
study.locator: arXiv:2410.21680v2, Sections 2 and 5: RSC cluster design, failure taxonomy and MTTF analysis with scheduler-side requeue metrics
study.depth: Model goodput for one job size only. Do not merge these research-cluster numbers with Llama 3 production counts.

focus: Strong scaling fixes the global problem and grows ranks. Weak scaling grows the problem with ranks, usually tokens per GPU. Efficiency is speedup over ranks, or throughput over ranks versus the baseline.
Goodput discounts failed, repeated and unusable work: restarts, preemption, straggler idle and checkpoint overhead. Busy GPUs doing repeated work raise utilization but not goodput.
Failure rate grows with job size, so large jobs pay more checkpoint and restart tax. Every MTTF number is cluster-specific.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, compute strong-scaling efficiency for \(T_1 = 100\) ms and \(T_4 = 30\) ms: speedup \(100/30 \approx 3.33\), efficiency \(3.33/4 \approx 83\) percent. Then state goodput at 90 percent effective time as \(0.9\) times raw throughput.
traps: Quoting weak-scaling efficiency without stating what is held fixed per rank (tokens, batch or model shard).
Merging interruption counts across studies. Llama 3 Table 5 and the Meta reliability MTTF come from different clusters and mixes.
Treating device utilization as useful throughput when restarts, retries and straggler idle consume the hours.

selfTest.q: What is fixed in strong scaling versus weak scaling?
selfTest.a: Strong scaling fixes the global problem size. Weak scaling grows it with ranks, typically holding tokens or work per rank fixed.

selfTest.q: Four ranks cut step time from 100 ms to 30 ms. What are speedup and efficiency?
selfTest.a: Speedup \(100/30 \approx 3.33\). Efficiency \(3.33/4 \approx 83\) percent against the single-rank baseline.

selfTest.q: How can utilization read 90 percent while goodput is poor?
selfTest.a: GPUs stay busy on repeated, failed or unusable work: restarts after interruptions, straggler waiting, and checkpoint overhead all count as utilized but not useful.

selfTest.q: Why does MTTF fall as job size grows, and what follows for checkpointing?
selfTest.a: More components mean more chances per hour that one fails. Larger jobs need cheaper checkpoints and faster restart because interruptions arrive sooner.

study.title: Continuous benchmarking and logging
study.locator: Chapter 13, Continuous Integration and Performance Benchmarking, with the HUD performance dashboard and MLPerf logging sections

focus: A fixed workload names model, data, global batch, sequence, precision and a correctness check. The Ultra-Scale heatmaps compare configs at one fixed 1M-token workload, never across workloads.
Warmup settles compilation, allocator and cache state. `torch.cuda.synchronize` and a cross-rank barrier separate launch from work. Report raw samples with median and spread from repeated trials.
A manifest records workload hash, config, code version, hardware, backend, environment flags and raw samples. The correctness guard runs with every timing so a fast wrong result fails.
units.reproduce: From a blank file, write a benchmark harness for a tiny MLP step that warms up, synchronizes with `torch.cuda.synchronize`, times repeated trials, reports median and spread, and checks the result against a single-process reference within tolerance.
traps: Timing CUDA work without synchronization. Asynchronous launch returns early and measures queueing, not execution.
Reporting one trial or a mean without warmup. Compilation, allocator growth and cache state dominate the first steps.
Changing batch, precision or data between runs and calling the delta a speedup. Fix the workload first.

selfTest.q: Why must the workload stay fixed across a comparison?
selfTest.a: Step time, tokens/s and MFU all depend on model, batch, sequence and precision. Changing any of them changes the work, so the comparison measures a different job.

selfTest.q: What goes wrong when CUDA timing omits synchronization?
selfTest.a: Kernel launches are asynchronous, so the timer stops at enqueue time. The measured time is launch overhead, far below execution time.

selfTest.q: What does warmup settle, and what happens without it?
selfTest.a: Compilation, allocator blocks and cache state. Without warmup the first trials are slower and more variable, and the mean misleads.

selfTest.q: What belongs in a regression evidence manifest?
selfTest.a: Workload identity and hash, configuration, code version, hardware and topology, backend, environment flags, raw timing samples, and the correctness-guard result.
